design_detail: Two parts, from the Centre for Psychedelic Research at Imperial College London. (1) Prospective online cohort without a comparison group: adults who planned to attend a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD) signed up at psychedelicsurvey.com after online advertisements and answered a 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire written for the study (nine items form a 'Non-physicalist Beliefs' factor, NPB) and nine FAD-Plus items on free will and fatalistic determinism about one week before, and again 4 weeks and 6 months after, the ceremony; acute experience (one day after), absorption, peer conformity, identity fusion with the group and well-being were also measured. Analyses: Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests, tables of conversion between preferred positions, correlations of belief change with well-being change and an exploratory path model. (2) Secondary analysis of the phase 2 double-blind randomized trial of psilocybin therapy versus escitalopram for major depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03429075): a 5-item short version of the questionnaire at baseline and week 6 in 30 and 29 patients, repeated-measures ANCOVA with one-tailed tests (pp. 8-11). Appraised as a cohort with ROBINS-E because the paper's headline claims rest on the uncontrolled cohort; the trial part is described in the notes.
can_establish: Whether, among people who chose to attend a psychedelic ceremony and answered the follow-up surveys, agreement with non-physicalist statements (other realms, a non-natural unifying principle, panpsychism, mind-body dualism) was higher 4 weeks and 6 months afterwards than a week before, and by how much on a standardized scale; and, in one randomized trial, whether patients given psilocybin therapy shifted more on a short version of the same questions than patients given escitalopram.
cannot_establish: That the psychedelic caused the shift in the ceremony cohort (no comparison group; the ceremony's setting, group, ritual, teachings and expectations come with the drug, and about 85% of baseline respondents are missing from the paired analyses); that the trial shows a difference between psilocybin and escitalopram at the usual two-sided level (one-tailed p = 0.041, two-sided equivalent about 0.08); whether the new beliefs are true, which the study does not address; or whether the shifts persist beyond 6 months.

sample.recruitment: Cohort: online advertisements inviting people planning to attend a ceremony with a plant medicine (for example an ayahuasca retreat) or another guided psychedelic experience to sign up at the study website; automated email links one week before, one day after and 4 weeks after the indicated date, with the 6-month survey named under Measures (Methods › Design and participants, p. 8; Measures, p. 10). Trial: 59 patients with major depression recruited through trial networks, social media and other sources (p. 9).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohort: aged 18 or over, good comprehension of English, and the intention to take part in a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic (a 5-HT2A agonist such as psilocybin, DMT, mescaline or LSD); no exclusions stated (p. 8). Trial: HAM-D-17 above 17 at screening, aged 18-80; excluded personal or immediate family history of psychosis, medically significant conditions, serious suicide attempts, positive pregnancy test, MRI contraindications, current SSRIs or previous escitalopram (p. 9).
sample.demographics: Baseline cohort (Table 2, N = 819): age 44.4 (SD 12.6); 359 women (43.8%), 455 men (55.6%), 5 other; United States 43.8%, United Kingdom 19.5%; master's degree 33.6%, doctorate or professional degree 20.5%; White 90.7%; working full time 63.4%; median household income 9000 dollars a month (p. 9). Characteristics of the 122 analysed are in Supplementary Table 1, not among the files. Trial demographics are in the trial report (not read).
sample.attrition: Of 819 (Table 2) or 866 (Results) baseline respondents, 122 contributed paired NPB data at both 4 weeks and 6 months (t(121) at both time points; about 14-15%, editors' calculation); completers were not compared with dropouts. Other analyses used different, unstated samples: the r and p values in Figure 3 imply about 370 respondents at 4 weeks and about 140 at 6 months (editors' calculation), and a 0.8% cell in Figure 2 implies at least about 118 baseline dualists in the 4-week conversion analysis (editors' inference). Trial: 59 patients (30 and 29).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected attendees of psychedelic ceremonies and retreats, mostly from Western countries, highly educated and with high incomes, who already leaned towards non-physicalist positions at baseline (Figure 1b, p. 3: baseline means on the agree side for the transcendentalism, non-naturalism, panpsychism and dualism items and on the disagree side for materialism). Religious affiliation and interest in metaphysical questions were not recorded; the authors say the sample may be skewed towards people sensitive to these belief shifts (Discussion, 14th paragraph, p. 8). With about 85% missing from the paired analyses and no comparison of completers with dropouts, the results describe completers only; if people whose beliefs shifted were more inclined to keep answering, the shifts would be overstated.

exposure.measurement: Cohort: self-reported attendance at a psychedelic ceremony; the substance, amount and setting were participants' own choices and are not reported in this paper (study details in Kettner et al., 2021, not read). One day after: Mystical Experience Questionnaire, visual scales of the 11-dimension Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire and the Perceived Emotional Synchrony Scale; at baseline: absorption (MODTAS) and peer conformity (four items of the short suggestibility scale); identity fusion with the ceremony group (one pictorial item) shortly before the session. Where a respondent attended more than one ceremony and gave several reports, only the largest score on each scale was used (pp. 10-11).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cohort: not controlled and not reported. Trial (study conditions): psilocybin 25 mg on two dosing days plus 6 weeks of daily placebo, or psilocybin 1 mg on the two days plus daily escitalopram (p. 9).

comparison.controls: Cohort: none; beliefs compared within person over time. A cross-sectional association with lifetime psychedelic use at baseline (Spearman r = 0.223). Trial: randomized comparison of psilocybin therapy with escitalopram, both with psychological support, on a 5-item short version of the questionnaire.
comparison.matching: Not applicable in the cohort. Trial: ANCOVA adjusted for baseline NPB (p. 11).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Religious affiliation, prior spiritual practice, interest in metaphysics, environmental susceptibilities, the beliefs of co-attendees, facilitators and trial staff, and the teachings offered at ceremonies were not measured; the authors call the failure to measure the cultural milieu an oversight (Discussion, 14th and 15th paragraphs, p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire (MBQ): 13 agree-disagree statements, ten written for the study and three from earlier research; an exploratory factor analysis at baseline kept one factor of nine items with loadings above 0.4 in absolute value, labelled Non-physicalist Beliefs (NPB), Cronbach's alpha 0.86 (Table 1, p. 2). Nine items of the FAD-Plus free-will and fatalistic-determinism subscales. Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months. Trial: five MBQ items (ontological and supernatural transcendentalism, dualism, materialism, non-naturalism) and the Universality subscale of the Spiritual Transcendence Scale at baseline and week 6 (Methods › Measures, p. 10).
outcomes.validity_norms: The MBQ is new; its only psychometric evidence here is the baseline factor analysis and alpha, and the authors say the relationship between items and philosophical positions could be contested, so items are best treated at face value (p. 2). No norms. The 5-item trial version has no reported reliability.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Shift away from physicalism' = an increase in the NPB factor score. 'Conversion' = a change in which of three items (materialism, dualism, idealism) a respondent endorsed most, with ties or no positive endorsement classed as none/mixed; for panpsychism, believers, sceptics and neutral by one item (pp. 10-11).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: The paper names two main outcome measures (the MBQ and the FAD-Plus items, p. 10); paired comparisons and item-level and conversion tests are Bonferroni-corrected, but there is no correction across scales, correlations or the path model. The trial analyses report one-tailed p values, justified by hypotheses derived from the survey data (p. 11).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable for the online self-report cohort. Trial: double-blind allocation; whether patients could tell their treatment is not reported in this paper.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cohort, NPB, all respondents (n = 122): 4 weeks t(121) = 3.66, Bonferroni p = 0.001, d = 0.33; 6 months t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46 (printed 95% CIs [0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50]; editors' 95% CIs for d about 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65, see reporting issues). Psychedelic-naive (n = 53): d = 0.53 at 4 weeks and 0.73 at 6 months. Fatalistic determinism, all: d = 0.25 at 4 weeks (p = 0.012), no persisting change at 6 months; naive: d = 0.46 and 0.39 (p. 3). Baseline NPB and lifetime psychedelic use: Spearman r = 0.223, p < 0.0001; fatalism r = 0.186 (p. 3). Conversion (Figure 2, p. 4): of baseline 'hard materialists', 24.4% remained at 4 weeks and 22.2% at 6 months (31.1% and 33.3% moved to dualism, 42.2% and 44.4% to none/mixed); of baseline dualists, 55.5% and 65.2% remained (37% and 23.9% moved to none/mixed); of respondents neutral on panpsychism, 57.3% and 54.5% became believers. Well-being: NPB change correlated with well-being change r = 0.2 (p = 0.0001) at 4 weeks and r = 0.18 (p = 0.033) at 6 months (Figure 3, p. 5). Path model, standardized betas to the 4-week NPB score: emotional synchrony 0.22, moderated by peer conformity (0.08); synchrony predicted by identity fusion 0.30, absorption 0.18, gender -0.17, age -0.12 and baseline NPB 0.13 (Figure 4, p. 5). Trial: drug by time interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed (editors' calculation: two-sided p = 0.082); psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45; escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2; psilocybin responders vs escitalopram responders Z = 1.74, p = 0.041, Hedges' g = 0.56, 90% CI -0.17 to 1.26; in the psilocybin arm NPB change correlated with change in spiritual universality r = 0.52, p = 0.003 (pp. 5-6; Figure 5).
analysis.covariates: None for the paired tests and correlations; the path model contained the variables listed above; the trial ANCOVA adjusted for baseline NPB.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned for the cohort analyses. The trial is registered (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03429075, EudraCT 2017-000219-18; p. 10), but the paper does not say whether the belief items were a registered outcome; the registry was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The analytic sample of each analysis is not stated and differs between analyses; the path model kept only predictors with significant effects (mystical-type and visual scores were dropped for non-significance, p. 11); in the trial, psilocybin responders are compared with escitalopram responders rather than with non-responders, which is what the Discussion describes; the correlation with spiritual universality is not reported numerically for the escitalopram arm; supplementary results were not read.
analysis.power: No power calculation for either part.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 122 ceremony attendees who answered both follow-ups, agreement with non-physicalist statements was modestly higher 4 weeks (d = 0.33) and 6 months (d = 0.46) after the ceremony than a week before, more so in 53 respondents taking a psychedelic for the first time (d = 0.53 and 0.73); respondents already leaned this way at baseline. Fatalism rose at 4 weeks only. Positions shifted in both directions in the conversion tables (for example 17.6% of none/mixed respondents moved towards materialism at 4 weeks), but most baseline materialists moved away from materialism and many neutral respondents became panpsychist 'believers'. Belief change correlated weakly with well-being change (r about 0.2). In the trial, patients given psilocybin shifted on a 5-item version (d = 0.45) and patients given escitalopram less (d = 0.2), with a group difference significant only one-tailed (two-sided p about 0.08).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title states that psychedelics 'alter' metaphysical beliefs; the abstract that the findings 'imply that psychedelic-use may causally influence metaphysical beliefs' and that the shifts were consolidated by an independent controlled trial; the Discussion that psychedelic use may be a key 'casual' [sic] determinant of the shifts (p. 6). Gaps: (1) the cohort has no comparison group and ceremonies bundle the drug with group, ritual and teaching; the authors concede that views held by co-attendees and research staff may have transferred (p. 8); (2) the abstract calls the sample large, but the paired analyses rest on 122 of more than 800 baseline respondents; (3) the abstract says the changes were positively correlated with the extent of past psychedelic use, but the reported correlation is with baseline beliefs, a cross-sectional association, not with change; (4) in the trial the interaction is one-tailed (two-sided p about 0.08), the escitalopram arm moved in the same direction (d = 0.2), and the statement that belief change is specific to psychedelics rests on a correlation significant in one arm and not reported for the other; (5) the Discussion says the trial found belief shifts in psilocybin responders versus non-responders, whereas the Results compared psilocybin responders with escitalopram responders, with a 90% CI for g that includes zero; (6) the path model is exploratory, yet the Discussion says emotional synchrony 'strongly mediated' the shifts (beta 0.22, no indirect-effect test reported). The authors do decline to judge the value of the beliefs, note links between some non-physicalist beliefs and avoidant coping, and raise informed-consent implications (pp. 7-8).

timeline.event: Griffiths et al.: retrospective survey of 'God encounter' experiences, among the earlier retrospective evidence this paper cites (ref. 29).
Davis et al.: retrospective survey of entity encounters after inhaled DMT, one of the anecdotal, qualitative and retrospective reports this paper cites as hinting at belief change (p. 2).
Carhart-Harris et al.: phase 2 randomized trial of psilocybin therapy versus escitalopram for major depression, the source of this paper's trial data.

Nayak & Griffiths: retrospective survey of 1,606 people who attributed a belief change to a psychedelic experience; larger shares agreed after than (as recalled) before that animals, plants, fungi, objects and the universe can be conscious; cites this study.

replication.where_it_stands: Among the sources read for this card, this is the only prospective study of metaphysical belief change after psychedelic use, and its trial component the only randomized comparison; a retrospective survey reports shifts in the same direction for attributing consciousness to other entities (Nayak & Griffiths, 2022). The status is partial because the paper's own trial component points the same way but at one-tailed significance, and no independent prospective replication with a comparison group has been read.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests (p. 13).
funding.affiliations_note: Five authors from the Centre for Psychedelic Research and related units at Imperial College London (R.L. Carhart-Harris also at Neuroscape, University of California, San Francisco) and one philosopher from the Universities of Western Australia and Adelaide. The trial data come from the same group's trial. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study that measures metaphysical beliefs with a validated instrument before and after in people who take a psychedelic and in a comparison group attending similar retreats or ceremonies without one, records the teachings and the beliefs of facilitators and co-attendees, follows dropouts and pre-registers its analyses; and randomized trials with belief change as a pre-specified, two-sided outcome and a check on whether patients could tell their treatment.

domains.note: No comparison group in the cohort: the drug cannot be separated from the ceremony's setting, group, ritual and teachings, from expectations or from time. The trial part has randomization but a short, unvalidated version of the questionnaire and one-tailed tests.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Attendance is self-reported; the substance, amount and setting are not reported; for people attending more than one ceremony only the largest acute-experience score was used.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: Self-selected ceremony attendees who already leaned towards non-physicalist positions; entry did not depend on the outcome, but the sample is atypical.

Integration practices, further ceremonies and contact with psychedelic communities after the ceremony were not recorded; the authors suggest cultural reinforcement may consolidate such beliefs (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, pp. 6-7).
About 85% of baseline respondents are missing from the paired analyses, without a comparison of completers and dropouts; respondents whose beliefs shifted may have been more likely to keep answering.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: A new questionnaire with face-value items, self-reported in a context where the direction of expected change is culturally familiar; repeated administration.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration mentioned; analytic samples differ between analyses and are not stated; the path model kept significant predictors only; one-tailed tests in the trial; the responder comparison is described differently in the Results and the Discussion.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three domains are high, and each could by itself produce the reported pattern: confounding by the ceremony context without any comparison group, heavy unanalysed attrition, and selective, inconsistently reported analyses. ROBINS-E rates the result very high when several domains are high in ways that substantially lower confidence. The prospective measurement of beliefs before the ceremony is a real strength over retrospective surveys. The card may be cited for the observed modest shifts among the 122 completers (d = 0.33 at 4 weeks and 0.46 at 6 months), for respondents already leaning non-physicalist at baseline, for shifts occurring in both directions in the conversion tables, and for the trial's one-tailed result stated with its two-sided equivalent; it should not be cited as showing that psychedelics cause belief change, that the change is specific to psychedelics, or that the beliefs are true or false.

key_findings.finding: The 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire yielded one factor of nine items, Non-physicalist Beliefs (Cronbach's alpha 0.86): positive loadings for another realm that can be visited (0.790), supernatural transition to other realms (0.740), a unifying principle beyond scientific explanation (0.776), panpsychism (0.642), primacy of other realms (0.592), dualism (0.444) and solipsism or idealism (0.441); negative loadings for materialism (-0.727) and naturalism (-0.598).

Among respondents with paired data (t(121), that is 122 people by the editors' reading of the degrees of freedom), NPB scores shifted away from physicalism from a week before to 4 weeks after the ceremony (t(121) = 3.66, p = 0.001, d = 0.33) and to 6 months after (t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46).
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs, 3rd paragraph (p. 2, continuing on p. 3); Figure 1a (p. 3)
key_findings.note: The printed 95% CIs ([0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50]) are not CIs of d; editors' 95% CIs for d are about 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65. 122 is about 15% of the 819 in Table 2 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Respondents having their first psychedelic experience (t(52), that is 53 people by the editors' reading of the degrees of freedom; the n is not printed) shifted more: d = 0.53 at 4 weeks (t(52) = 3.85, p = 0.001) and d = 0.73 at 6 months (t(52) = 5.32, p < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs, 3rd paragraph (continued from p. 2)

key_findings.finding: At the item level, Figure 1b marks a significant change at 6 months (**) for ontological transcendentalism, supernatural transcendentalism, materialism (down), panpsychism and dualism, and at 4 weeks only (*) for non-naturalism and primacy of other realms; naturalism and solipsism or idealism carry no significance marker. At baseline the means already lay on the agree side for the transcendentalism, non-naturalism, panpsychism, primacy and dualism items and on the disagree side for materialism, naturalism and solipsism or idealism.
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 1b; the item axis runs from Disagree to Agree without numbers, so item changes cannot be given in scale units. The legend lists solipsism/idealism among items that changed, but the figure gives it no marker (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Fatalistic determinism rose at 4 weeks in all respondents (t(121) = 2.81, p = 0.012, d = 0.25) but not at 6 months; in psychedelic-naive respondents it rose at 4 weeks (d = 0.46, p = 0.003) and 6 months (d = 0.39, p = 0.012).

At baseline, more lifetime psychedelic use went with stronger non-physicalist beliefs (Spearman r = 0.223, p < 0.0001) and with stronger fatalistic determinism (r = 0.186, p < 0.0001); in item terms with stronger panpsychist (r = 0.19) and weaker materialist views (r = -0.18). These are cross-sectional associations, not changes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs, 3rd paragraph and Fatalism, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Figure 1a (right panel); Figure 2e (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Conversion between preferred positions (Figure 2): of baseline 'hard materialists', 24.4% still held that position at 4 weeks and 22.2% at 6 months; 31.1% and 33.3% moved to dualism and 42.2% and 44.4% to none/mixed. Of baseline dualists, 55.5% and 65.2% remained; 37% and 23.9% moved to none/mixed. Shifts also ran towards materialism: 17.6% (4 weeks) and 15.2% (6 months) of none/mixed respondents moved there. Of respondents neutral on panpsychism, 57.3% (4 weeks) and 54.5% (6 months) became believers; 83.9% and 86.8% of baseline believers remained believers.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2a-d and legend; Results › Conversion of preferred metaphysical beliefs, 1st paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4)
key_findings.note: The group sizes behind the percentages are not printed; the chi-squared statistics are shown only as asterisks.

key_findings.finding: Shifts towards non-physicalist beliefs correlated weakly with increases in well-being (WEMWBS): r = 0.2, p = 0.0001 at 4 weeks and r = 0.18, p = 0.033 at 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs and well-being, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: These r and p values imply about 370 and about 140 respondents (editors' calculation), not the 122 of the paired analyses.

key_findings.finding: Exploratory path model (standardized betas): perceived emotional synchrony with the group during the session predicted the 4-week NPB score (0.22), moderated by baseline peer conformity (0.08); synchrony was predicted by identity fusion with the group shortly before the session (0.30), trait absorption (0.18), gender (-0.17), age (-0.12) and baseline NPB (0.13); baseline NPB predicted 4-week NPB with beta 0.75. Mystical-type and visual-effect scores were dropped from the model for non-significance.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4 and legend; Results › Process of change modelling, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Methods › Statistical analysis, path-analysis paragraph (p. 11)
key_findings.note: The coding of gender is not stated in the main text; model fit is in Supplementary Table 2 (not read).

key_findings.finding: Trial (psilocybin therapy n = 30, escitalopram n = 29, 5-item NPB at baseline and week 6): drug by time interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed; within-arm change psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45, escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2; psilocybin responders shifted more than escitalopram responders (Z = 1.74, p = 0.041, g = 0.56, 90% CI -0.17 to 1.26); in the psilocybin arm NPB change correlated with change in spiritual universality (r = 0.52, p = 0.003).
key_findings.locator: Results › Validation with data from a controlled clinical trial, 1st paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6); Figure 5 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: F(1, 56) = 3.13 has a two-sided p of 0.082. See reporting issues on the escitalopram and responder statistics.

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: religious affiliation, environmental susceptibilities and interest in metaphysical beliefs were not collected; the sample may be skewed towards people sensitive to these shifts; both samples were largely Western and well educated; the two samples differ in size, distress and expectations; views held by co-attendees and trial staff, or the wider psychedelic culture, may have transferred to participants.

The authors say that services and studies offering psychedelic experiences may be ethically obliged to mention possible belief change in informed consent, and that it would be hasty to read the findings as showing that non-physicalist, panpsychist or fatalistic beliefs are of positive value, noting associations of some such beliefs with avoidant coping ('spiritual bypassing').

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say 866 respondents completed the belief survey at different time points, Table 2 gives 819 at baseline, and the paired analyses have 121 degrees of freedom (122 people) at both 4 weeks and 6 months; the abstract calls the sample large.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline belief shifts rest on about 15% of the baseline sample, and the main text does not say who the 122 were or how they compared with those who dropped out (Supplementary Table 1, cited for sample characteristics, was not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CIs printed next to the d values (d = 0.33 with [0.12, 0.39]; d = 0.46 with [0.22, 0.50]; d = 0.73 with [0.36, 0.80]) cannot be CIs of d: several sit asymmetrically around d or barely include it; editors' 95% CIs for d = 0.33 and 0.46 with n = 122 are about 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65. They are probably CIs of the raw mean change, whose scale is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The intervals should not be quoted as uncertainty around the effect sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: Analytic samples differ between analyses and are not stated: in Figure 3, r = 0.2 with p = 0.0001 implies about 370 respondents at 4 weeks and r = 0.18 with p = 0.033 about 140 at 6 months (editors' calculation); in Figure 2, 0.8% of baseline dualists at 4 weeks implies at least about 118 dualists in that analysis, more than the 122 respondents of the paired analyses could supply alongside the other groups (editors' inference).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analyses do not describe one cohort; the well-being correlations and conversion tables cannot be linked to the paired belief changes.

reporting_issues.issue: The trial interaction is printed as F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 'one-tailed'; with 1 and 56 degrees of freedom this F gives p = 0.082 two-sided (editors' calculation). One-tailed testing is justified by hypotheses from the survey (p. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: At the conventional two-sided level the psilocybin-escitalopram difference in belief change is not significant; the 'validation' is weaker than the abstract's word 'consolidated' suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: For the escitalopram arm, Z = 0.24 is printed with p = 0.33 and d = 0.2; Z = 0.24 corresponds to a one-tailed p of 0.41 (0.81 after the Bonferroni doubling applied to the psilocybin arm's Z = 2.28, p = 0.02), and a d of 0.2 in 29 patients would usually go with a larger Z (about 1.1 if d is the within-person standardized change; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the three escitalopram statistics is misprinted; the escitalopram change may be larger than 'no changes' suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The responder comparison is significant one-tailed (Z = 1.74, p = 0.041), yet its 90% CI for g (-0.17 to 1.26), the interval that matches a one-tailed 5% test, includes zero. The Methods describe a comparison of 'remitters', the Results of 'responders' (a fall of at least 50%), and the Discussion of psilocybin responders against non-responders.
reporting_issues.consequence: What was compared, and whether it is significant, is unclear; the number of responders per arm is not given.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the belief changes were positively correlated with the extent of past psychedelic use, but the Results report a correlation between lifetime use and baseline beliefs.
reporting_issues.consequence: A cross-sectional association is presented as if it concerned change.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor: in Table 2, 250 with a college diploma is printed as 30.1% (250 of 819 is 30.5%), and the ethnicity rows sum to 840 against a total of 819 (editors' arithmetic); the Figure 1 legend lists solipsism/idealism among items that changed, but the figure marks no significant change for it; the gender coding of the path model is not stated, although the Discussion says female gender predicted the shifts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; none changes the main findings.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, open access CC BY), Scientific Reports 11, article 22166, pp. 1-13 (all pages; Tables 1-2 and Figures 1-5 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Figure 1 panels read on a 300-dpi crop). The Supplementary Information (Supplementary Results, Supplementary Tables 1-2, Supplementary Figures 1-4, Supplementary Methods with the FAD-Plus and spirituality items) is not among the files and was not read; neither were Kettner et al. (2021, the cohort's parent report) or the trial report. Read by AI reader 673. Discussion paragraphs are counted as running text from the Discussion heading on p. 6.
